meaning: Satoshi Nakamoto is the name under which Bitcoin was described in 2008 and its first software released; the identity of the person or people behind the name is unknown.

meaning: Node resources are the things that a node consumes in order to do its work: time and bandwidth to download the chain, disk space to store it, memory to keep the data it needs often, and network connections to other nodes

meaning: A pruned node deletes old blocks to reduce disk use while still downloading and verifying the whole chain; automatic pruning needs a target of at least 550 MiB.

meaning: A peer is another node with which a node keeps a connection to exchange blocks and transactions; a node limits how many it keeps.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The set of unspent transaction outputs is the compact record of everything that can still be spent; a node updates it for every block and it is the data that the database cache holds.

meaning: A release tag marks a snapshot of the source by version number; release candidates carry the suffix rc and stable releases none.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Source code is the human-readable text of a program, mainly C++ in Bitcoin Core, from which the executables are built; it can be read and audited by anyone.

meaning: Git is a distributed version control system; cloning copies the whole repository with its history and a commit is named by a long hash.

meaning: Release candidates, intended for testing, carry the suffix rc; stable releases that can run on production systems have no suffix.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The toolchain group gathers the programs and conventions that turn source code into running executables: the build system, which decides how, the compilation, which does the translation, the prerequisites, which must be present, and the executables, which are the result

meaning: A package manager installs software and the libraries it depends on from a collection maintained for an operating system or a build.

meaning: Configuration is the group of concepts that describe how a user tells Bitcoin Core how to behave
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Configuration

meaning: Bitcoin Core reads bitcoin.conf from its data directory at every start; options can also be given on the command line, and bitcoind -printtoconsole shows where the file is looked for.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An option has a name and a value and can come from the file, from the dynamic settings file or from the command line; the command line wins.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The data directory is where Bitcoin Core keeps the blocks, the unspent-output database, the logs and the wallets; its default place depends on the system and its contents on the network.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The dbcache option sizes the cache of the unspent-output set: 450 MiB by default in the book, 1024 MiB by default from Bitcoin Core 31.0 on machines with enough memory.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The txindex option builds an index of every transaction so that getrawtransaction can find any of them; it cannot be combined with pruning.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: In blocks-only mode a node accepts blocks from its peers but not unconfirmed transactions, which saves bandwidth and memory.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The maxmempool option limits the memory used for unconfirmed transactions; the default is 300 megabytes, and unused mempool memory is lent to the database cache.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The alertnotify option runs a command of the owner's choice when the node raises an alert, replacing %s with the message, which the node first cleans and puts in single quotes.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Running is the group of concepts that describe a node while it is alive: how it is started so that it keeps going without a person, what it writes while it starts, and how its owner asks two short questions about its state
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Running

meaning: A daemon is a program that runs in the background; bitcoind -daemon detaches from the terminal, and init scripts such as the systemd unit start it at boot and restart it after a failure.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: While it starts, the node prints a log of what it is setting up: its version, the settings read, the connection limits, the interface it opens, the wallet database and the cache sizes.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The getblockchaininfo call reports the chain the node follows: its name, the number of blocks and headers, the best block, its difficulty and chain work, whether the node is still in its initial download and whether it is pruned.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The getnetworkinfo call reports the node's own version, the protocol version, the services it offers, its connections and reachable networks, and the fee rates it uses to accept transactions.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The wallet group collects the concepts about the wallet that comes with Bitcoin Core
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Wallet

meaning: The current default wallet is a descriptor wallet stored in SQLite; legacy BerkeleyDB wallets can no longer be created or loaded and can only be migrated.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The legacy wallet was stored in a Berkeley DB file and described by its keys; since Bitcoin Core 30.0 it can no longer be created or loaded, only migrated.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An output descriptor is a short text that describes a set of output scripts, optionally followed by an 8-character checksum that detects typing and copying errors.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An output type is the form of locking an output uses, such as P2PKH, P2SH-P2WPKH, P2WPKH and P2TR, and a descriptor wallet keeps one descriptor for each type it supports.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The interface branch is about how other programs and people talk to a running node
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node

meaning: The RPC interface is the group of concepts that describe the programmatic doorway of Bitcoin Core
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel RpcInterface

meaning: An application programming interface is the set of requests that one program offers to other programs; Bitcoin Core's API lets a program ask the node about the chain, the mempool and the wallet.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Bitcoin Core's API is JSON-RPC over HTTP, by default to 127.0.0.1 on port 8332, so any program that can make an HTTP request can call it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: JSON is a text format for structured data made of objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null; every answer of Bitcoin Core's API is written in it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: HTTP is the request-and-response protocol of the web; Bitcoin Core receives each JSON-RPC call as the body of an HTTP POST request and sends the answer as the body of the HTTP response.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: By default Bitcoin Core creates a random credential on each start and stores it in the data directory as .cookie, which bitcoin-cli reads; rpcauth.py makes a static credential instead.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The rpcauth option holds a user name, a random salt and the HMAC-SHA256 of the password under that salt, so the file never contains the password itself.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A salt is a random value mixed into the hashing of a password, so that equal passwords give different stored values.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: An HMAC is a hash computed with a secret key, so that only someone who knows the key can produce or check the value.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The client group collects the concepts about the programs that call the interface
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Client

meaning: The command line is a text interface in which a person types the name of a program followed by arguments and reads the program's text output.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The bitcoin-cli helper sends the same calls the API offers, which makes it the way to experiment interactively; its help command lists the available RPC commands.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A wrapper library hides the HTTP call: python-bitcoinlib's RawProxy turns p.getblockchaininfo() into the JSON-RPC request and returns the decoded answer.

meaning: The data branch is about what a node holds and what the interface shows of it: the transactions that move value, the blocks that gather them into the shared record, and the state of the chain that results

meaning: The transaction group collects the concepts about the objects that carry value
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; picture; table

meaning: Serialization writes a transaction as a sequence of bytes, with a marker and a flag before the inputs when the transaction has witness data, shown in hexadecimal notation.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Decoding the serialized hexadecimal of Alice's payment shows its one input, two outputs, addresses and script types, exactly as the chain holds them.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Segregated witness moves the signature data of a transaction out of the part that the identifier covers, into a witness that counts less toward the size limit.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A transaction's weight counts its non-witness bytes four times and its witness bytes once, and its virtual size is the weight divided by four, rounded up.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual TransactionWeight; lab example

meaning: The txid hashes the transaction without its witness and the hash includes it; a txid is not authoritative before confirmation because a transaction can be modified.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Malleability is the possibility that a transaction is modified before confirmation so that its identifier changes while its meaning does not; the witness separation removed it for the txid of witness spends.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The block group collects the concepts about the unit in which transactions are recorded
slide visual: code; drawn shapes; native chart; picture; table
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Block

meaning: A block is found by its height, how many blocks precede it, or by its header hash; its confirmations count the blocks built on top, itself included.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The block hash is the double SHA-256 hash of the 80-byte block header, written backwards; it identifies a block uniquely and is not stored in the block.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The block header holds the version, the previous block hash, the Merkle root, the timestamp, the compact target and the nonce, in 80 bytes.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; chapter visual BlockHeader; lab example

meaning: A block without witness data weighs four times its size in weight units, which the getblock result shows as size, strippedsize and weight.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The Merkle root in a block header commits to every transaction of the block, and hashing the block's transaction identifiers pairwise up to one value reproduces it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The subsidy starts at 50 bitcoins and is shifted right once for every 210,000 blocks, so it is 6.25 bitcoins at height 775072.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The bits field is a four-byte compact form of the target: the first byte is the length in bytes and the next three are the leading digits, so the target is the digits shifted left by the length minus three bytes.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A block's difficulty follows from its bits, the compact form of its target, as the ratio of the easiest target to this block's target.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The median time past is the middle value of the timestamps of the last 11 blocks, which the consensus rules use as the clock for time limits because a single miner cannot move it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The chain state group collects the concepts that describe the blocks as a whole: which chain is the true one, how much work it represents, how deep a block is in it, and what happens when the node changes its mind
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel ChainState

meaning: The best chain is the valid chain with the most cumulative proof of work; it is not necessarily the one with the most blocks.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: The work of a block is 2^256 divided by its target plus one, the expected number of hashes needed to find it, and the chain work is the sum of the work of all blocks up to it.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A confirmation counts the blocks from a transaction's block to the tip, itself included; each one makes it harder to reverse the transaction.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A reorganization occurs when a node switches to a different chain with more work: blocks leave the best chain, their transactions return to the mempool unless the new chain includes them, and the set of unspent outputs is updated.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A fork is a split of the chain into two branches, accidental when two miners find blocks at about the same time, or permanent when rules change incompatibly.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A downloaded release can be checked against the SHA-256 checksums the project publishes and the signatures on them, which shows that the file matches the published record and not that the signers' keys are trustworthy.

meaning: A checksum is a short fixed-size value computed from a file by a hash function, so that any change to the file makes the value change.

meaning: An OpenPGP signature is a digital signature in the format of the OpenPGP standard, made with a person's secret key over a file and checked with the matching public key.

meaning: A reproducible build produces bit-for-bit identical files from the same source, so that several builders can independently attest to the same checksums.

meaning: A package registry is a public index of the software libraries published for a programming language, with each library's versions and release dates.

meaning: A JSON-LD context maps the keys of a JSON text to IRIs, so that the same JSON becomes linked data without changing its shape.

meaning: Representation is the group of concepts about how a program writes information down

carried by: divider and map slides (branch or section node)

meaning: A bit is a binary digit, a byte is eight bits and holds one of 256 values, so it is written with two hexadecimal digits.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A bit shift moves the bits of an integer to the left or to the right, which multiplies it by a power of two or divides it by one, dropping what falls off.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Unix time counts the seconds since 1 January 1970 at 00:00 UTC, and Bitcoin uses it for the times in block headers.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A random number is a value that nobody can predict, which Bitcoin Core draws from the computer's secure sources of randomness for cookies and salts.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Base64 is a way of writing bytes as text with 64 characters, so that binary data can travel in a text header, and it is not encryption.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: Systems is the group of concepts about where programs run and how they meet
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; panel Systems

meaning: A file holds data under a name, a directory holds files and other directories, and a path names a place in that hierarchy.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A process is a running program with its own memory, and a thread is a flow of execution inside a process that shares its memory with the others.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A library is a collection of code written to be used by other programs, which saves them from writing it again and which they load or compile in.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A database stores data so that it can be searched and updated reliably, and Bitcoin Core uses a key-value database for the chain and an SQL database for the wallet.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A platform is the combination of processor family and operating system for which a program is built, and a release has one archive for each.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A network protocol is an agreed format and order of messages between programs, such as HTTP between a client and a server, and a port number names the service on a machine.

meaning: A software test runs a program on chosen inputs and compares the result with the expected one, and Bitcoin Core requires its tests to pass before a change is merged.
page visualisation: concept map node; ontology graph node; lab example

meaning: A programming language is a notation for instructing a computer, and the chapter meets C++ for the node, Python for tests, helpers and examples, and the languages of the toolkits.
